title: Disapproving the behavior of Representative Jesús G. Chuy García of Illinois.
official_title: Disapproving the behavior of Representative Jesús G. Chuy García of Illinois.
likelihoodReason: Adopted by the House 236-183 with 4 voting present (Roll no. 292) on November 18, 2025. A simple resolution takes effect on House adoption — no Senate or presidential action is involved. Sponsored by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA), a member of García's own party, with no cosponsors.
summary: The House went on record disapproving the behavior of Rep. Jesús "Chuy" García of Illinois. The resolution recounts that García filed for reelection, that his chief of staff filed as the only other Democrat on the last day of filing at his direction, and that García then withdrew after the deadline — leaving her the lone Democrat on the March 2026 primary ballot.
brief: Formally disapproves of Rep. Chuy García's conduct around Illinois primary ballot filing, finding he directed his chief of staff to file before he withdrew after the deadline.

top_lines.headline: Formal Rebuke
subs: House disapproves of Rep. García's behavior
Finds his actions beneath the dignity of his office

top_lines.headline: Ballot Timeline
subs: Chief of staff filed November 5, the last day
García withdrew November 6, after the deadline

sections.label: Resolved Clause — Disapproval of Representative García

items.main: Places the House on record disapproving the behavior of the Representative from Illinois, Mr. García.
items.detail: The resolution's findings state that García filed nominating petitions on October 27, 2025 for the March 2026 Democratic primary; that his chief of staff, Patty Garcia, submitted her own paperwork on November 5, the last day of filing; that on November 6 — after the filing deadline — García confirmed he would not seek another term and would withdraw his petitions; and that his chief of staff was the only Democrat who filed, at his direction, which the findings describe as undermining the process of a free and fair election.

gaps: The resolution disapproves of the behavior but imposes no sanction, referral, or further action.
The findings describe the conduct as undermining a free and fair election, but the resolution directs no election-related remedy.
The resolution states the chief of staff filed at Representative García's direction but cites no investigation or source for that finding.

added: Formal House record of disapproval of Representative García's behavior

title: Directing the Committee on Ethics to preserve and publicly release records relating to monetary settlements involving acts of sexual harassment.
official_title: Directing the Committee on Ethics to preserve and publicly release records relating to monetary settlements involving acts of sexual harassment.
likelihoodReason: Adopted by the House 420-0 with 1 voting present (Roll no. 233) on June 30, 2026 — unanimous across both parties. A simple resolution takes effect on House adoption, and the 60-day disclosure clock runs from that date. Sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) with no cosponsors.
summary: Orders the House Ethics Committee and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights to publish, within 60 days, a list naming every House member whose sexual-harassment or sexual-abuse case ended in a taxpayer-funded payment — with the total amount shown next to each name. Aggregate totals must also be published for other taxpayer-funded settlements involving members and for House-employee cases.
brief: Requires public, name-by-name disclosure within 60 days of taxpayer-funded sexual-harassment settlements involving House members, plus aggregate totals for other member and employee settlements.

top_lines.headline: Naming Names
subs: Members with taxpayer-funded harassment settlements listed publicly
Total taxpayer amount shown next to each name
Disclosure due within 60 days of adoption

top_lines.headline: Aggregate Totals
subs: Totals disclosed for member settlements not involving harassment
House-employee settlement totals split the same way

top_lines.headline: What Counts
subs: Any settlement with a sexual-misconduct component counts in full

sections.label: Resolved Clauses — Public Release of Settlement Records

items.main: Requires a single consolidated public list naming each Member, Delegate, or Resident Commissioner who was the subject of a review or investigation involving sexual harassment under clause 9 or clause 18 of House Rule XXIII — or any sexual-harassment or sexual-abuse case — that resulted in a payment of taxpayer funds, with the total taxpayer amount adjacent to each name.
items.detail: The duty falls on the Committee on Ethics and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights for matters they reviewed, conducted, or facilitated, and the list is due not later than 60 days after adoption.

items.main: Requires aggregate totals of taxpayer funds paid in three other categories: member settlements with no sexual-misconduct component, House-employee settlements involving sexual harassment or abuse, and House-employee settlements not involving it.
items.detail: These categories are disclosed as lump totals rather than by name.

items.main: Counts a settlement as involving sexual harassment, abuse, or misconduct if that was any component of the matter, regardless of how the case was classified or resolved.
items.detail: This classification rule prevents matters from being excluded because they were settled under a different claim or category.

underreported.summary: Requires disclosure of aggregate taxpayer-funded settlement totals for matters that did not involve sexual harassment, covering both members and House employees.
underreported.why_unreported: The resolution's title concerns sexual-harassment settlement records, but these clauses also compel totals for every other kind of taxpayer-funded settlement, in aggregate.

gaps: Members are named individually, but House employees' settlements are disclosed only as aggregate totals.
The resolution sets a 60-day deadline but provides no enforcement mechanism if the committee or office misses it.
The disclosure covers names and amounts but not case details, dates, or the outcomes of the underlying investigations.
The resolution reaches matters the Ethics Committee or the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights handled, but does not address settlements resolved outside those two bodies.

added: Public, name-by-name disclosure of taxpayer-funded sexual-harassment settlements involving House members, with amounts, due within 60 days of adoption
Aggregate disclosure of other taxpayer-funded settlement totals for members and House employees
Classification rule counting any settlement with a sexual-misconduct component in full

title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon.
official_title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon.
likelihoodReason: Failed in the House 189-235 (Roll no. 232) on June 30, 2026. Sponsored by Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) with 43 cosponsors — a Democratic war-powers directive brought to the floor in a Republican-majority chamber, where the majority voted it down.
summary: Directs the President, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days of adoption. Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities could continue.
brief: Directs removal of U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days, with carve-outs for security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive
subs: Forces out of Lebanon hostilities within 7 days
Invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution

top_lines.headline: Carve-Outs
subs: Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces may continue
Nothing in it authorizes military force

sections.label: Section 1 — Removal of United States Armed Forces From Any Hostilities in Lebanon

items.main: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon no later than 7 days after adoption of the resolution, invoking section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution.
items.detail: The directive covers any hostilities in Lebanon, and the 7-day clock runs from the date the concurrent resolution is adopted.

items.main: Preserves security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and the protection of diplomatic facilities, and states that nothing in the resolution authorizes the use of military force.
items.detail: The non-authorization clause is stated to be consistent with section 8(a)(1) of the War Powers Resolution.

underreported.section: Section 2 — Rule of Construction Relating to Certain Activities
underreported.summary: Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities may continue even after forces are removed from hostilities.
underreported.why_unreported: The title reads as a full removal of U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon; the carve-out keeps two categories of U.S. military activity there running.

gaps: The resolution does not define which U.S. activities in Lebanon count as hostilities — the term that triggers removal.
The 7-day removal clock runs from adoption, but the resolution sets no reporting or verification requirement to confirm removal.
Security cooperation is preserved but not defined, leaving open how it differs from participation in hostilities.

added: Directive to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days of adoption
